**Claude:**

Same file, same size, one resolved path — the "two SIFs" theory is dead. That leaves your hypothesis standing as the best explanation, and it's a known FUSE behavior: **`squashfuse_ll` mounts the SIF as *you* (the invoking user), and a user-owned FUSE mount is only accessible by that user unless `allow_other` is set. If the sbatch path's apptainer starter stat's the rootfs as *root* (setuid mode), the kernel returns EPERM → "permission denied".** The salloc-interactive path evidently gets the loop-device (privileged) mount instead — likely because loop devices were free — which is why the identical command works there and 3/3 failed differently in sbatch. We can't fix `/etc/fuse.conf` (admin-owned), and we can't reliably control which mount mode a batch job gets.

So: stop mounting the SIF. Convert to a **sandbox directory** — a plain folder as the container rootfs, no FUSE, no squashfs, nothing left to EPERM:

```bash
# One-time, ~10-15 min, ~57 GB on $PROJECT (build from the registry:
# unprivileged-safe, avoids reading the SIF at all):
cd $PROJECT
apptainer build --sandbox dplm_sandbox docker://pieris98/dplm:cu121-torch220-cond

# Then point the scripts at it and resubmit — apptainer exec accepts a
# directory, so zero code changes:
export DPLM_SIF=$PROJECT/dplm_sandbox
sbatch scripts/meluxina/cond_dplm2_smoke.sbatch
tail -f logs/slurm/cond_dplm2_smoke_<JOBID>.out
```

Two notes:

- **Disk**: this puts a second 57 GB copy on `$PROJECT` (alongside the SIF). Once the smoke passes you can delete whichever you're not using — for production runs the sandbox is the one to keep.
- **Why this is the right endgame** rather than another flag: the flake (earlier `Terminating squashfuse_ll after timeout`) and the EPERM are two symptoms of the same fragile user-space SIF-mount layer. A directory rootfs eliminates the entire layer — container start becomes instant too (no squashfs mount), which slightly helps the 24h job as well.

If the build command fails on the login node (user-namespace restrictions vary), run the same `apptainer build --sandbox` from inside an allocation (`interactive.sh alloc` host shell) — it only needs CPU and a few minutes. And once the smoke passes on the sandbox, the same `export DPLM_SIF=...` carries straight into `sbatch scripts/meluxina/cond_dplm2_train.sbatch` for the full run.

## Audit result

**Already correct** (shared via `common.sh` / prior fixes): sandbox discovery, absolute `DPLM_PY`, account/qos, `SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR` root, retry wrapper for mount flakes, `.git` bind, env forwarding including `WANDB_*`, `++`-safe env-var overrides (`trainer.max_steps` / `train.lr` both exist in the config struct).

**Fixed now:**

| Issue | Fix |
|---|---|
| `--time=24:00:00` — 100K steps at `max_tokens 4000×4` likely exceeds 24h; job would die at the wall | Bumped to **3 days** (qos=long allows 6); checkpoints every 2000 steps make any interruption resumable |
| Checkpoint I/O: lm defaults are top-10 every 1000 steps, and each ckpt carries the full 650M state (~2.6 GB) → **~260 GB written**, GPU time stolen | Experiment yaml now **top-2 every 2000 steps** (~8 GB retained) |
| Header claimed `sbatch --nodes=2` works — it doesn't: the script launches one `python train.py` on the first node; node 2 would sit idle | Documented honestly as **single-node only**; multi-node needs an `srun`-based launch (not wired) |
| README's resume example used `trainer.resume_from_checkpoint=` without `++` — the *exact* struct-append bug that bit the smoke's `limit_val_batches` | Fixed to `++trainer.resume_from_checkpoint=` |

```bash

```

When you first followed the runbook's `cd $SCRATCH` (which didn't exist), bash's `cd` with an empty variable silently lands in `$HOME` — so the first 57 GB `apptainer pull` likely wrote `dplm_cond.sif` straight into `$HOME`. On top of that, `apptainer pull` keeps a **second full copy** of the downloaded OCI layers in `~/.cache/apptainer` and never cleans it up. Two copies of the image ≈ 100+ GB — that's your overage.

## Triage (run this, paste nothing — it's self-explanatory)

```bash
# Where is the space? Top offenders in $HOME:
du -h --max-depth=1 $HOME 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -15

# Confirm the usual suspects:
ls -lh $HOME/*.sif 2>/dev/null
du -sh ~/.cache/apptainer ~/.cache/huggingface ~/.cache/torch ~/.triton ~/.apptainer 2>/dev/null
```

## Cleanup, safe in this order

```bash
# 1. The duplicate SIF in $HOME (if present) — the real one lives in $PROJECT:
ls -lh /project/home/p201418/dplm_cond.sif          # confirm the keeper exists first
rm $HOME/dplm_cond.sif                              # ≈ −57 GB

# 2. Apptainer's layer cache — only needed to rebuild images; safe to nuke:
rm -rf ~/.cache/apptainer                           # ≈ −20–55 GB

# 3. Small strays, all regenerable:
rm -rf ~/.triton ~/.cache/torch ~/.cache/huggingface 2>/dev/null
```

That should bring you from 130 GiB to well under 20 GiB.

**One deliberate keep:** don't delete `$PROJECT/dplm_cond.sif` yet — even though the running training uses the sandbox, keep the SIF until the 100K-step run completes, as a fallback image. After it finishes you can reclaim another 57 GiB with `rm $PROJECT/dplm_cond.sif` (the sandbox at `$PROJECT/dplm_sandbox` is what the scripts prefer anyway).

If the `du` shows the space is somewhere unexpected instead (e.g. a stray wandb dir or old logs in `$HOME`), paste the top of the breakdown and I'll point at what's safe to drop.

**Claude:**

**No — the cache is not the same data as the `.sif`.** Three independent confirmations from your own output:

1. **The SIF is a self-contained squashfs archive.** When `apptainer pull` finishes, the SIF is written complete to `$PROJECT`; the cache blobs are the raw OCI layers (compressed tars) it downloaded along the way. No hardlinks — they're on *different filesystems* (`/home/users` vs `/mnt/tier2/project`), so the kernel couldn't even link them.
2. **There are two pulls' worth of layers in there.** The blob dates show a **Jul 20 set** (~33 G — the original base image pull) and an **Aug 28 set** (~26 G — the `-cond` image pull). The SIF only needed one of these; both stayed cached.
3. **The missing ~67 G is `oci-tmp`.** Your `du` of the blob dir says 60 G, but `~/.apptainer` totals 127 G — the difference sits in `cache/oci-tmp` (timestamped Aug 28 19:23, one minute before the SIF was written). That's the *extracted rootfs* from the pull: Apptainer unpacks the image to a temp sandbox before squashing it into the SIF, and an interrupted/abnormal cleanup left the whole thing behind.

So: ~60 G of layer blobs + ~67 G of pull remnant = your 127 G. All of it is rebuild-on-demand data.

## Cleanup

```bash
# see the remnant first (optional, confirms the theory):
du -sh ~/.apptainer/cache/oci-tmp

# the supported way — clears every cache subdir:
apptainer cache clean --all

# (equivalently: rm -rf ~/.apptainer/cache — same result)
```

Nothing you run depends on it: training uses the sandbox at `$PROJECT/dplm_sandbox` (different filesystem, untouched), the SIF at `$PROJECT` is untouched, and the only cost of deletion is re-downloading layers *if* you ever rebuild from `docker://` again.

Expected end state: `$HOME` drops from 131 G to ~4–5 G (just `.vscode-server`), comfortably under the 100 G quota. And as noted before — once the training run completes, `$PROJECT/dplm_cond.sif` (35 G) is also deletable, since the scripts prefer the sandbox.

i got logged out of meluxina. now i get this: kex_exchange_identification: read: Connection reset by peer

**Claude:**

> The user got logged out of Meluxina and now SSH fails with `kex_exchange_identification: read: Connection reset by peer` on port 8822.
> 
> This is a connection-level error BEFORE authentication — the TCP connection opens, but the remote side resets during the SSH identification/key-exchange banner exchange. Common causes:
> 
> 1. **Login node overloaded** — the login node was under heavy load (or their earlier processes?). But they were just doing light file ops.
> 2. **Fail2ban / security daemon banned their IP** — repeated rapid connections (VSCode server reconnects, multiple SSH sessions) can trigger rate-limiting. They connect via VSCode (`.vscode-server` present) and from changing IPs (last login from 45.66.41.127 — a VPN/proxy range?). Meluxina commonly has MaxStartups throttling (default 10:30:100) — unauthenticated connections dropped when too many pending.
> 3. **Transient network issue** on their side or the cluster's edge.
> 4. **Login node reboot/maintenance** — Meluxina occasionally reboots login nodes; connection reset during that.
> 5. The port 8822 is Meluxina's custom SSH port — correct.
> 
> Practical triage:
> 1. Wait 1–5 minutes and retry — transient resets usually clear.
> 2. Try the other login node by name if DNS round-robins (login01/02/03 — try `ssh -p 8822 login02.meluxina.luxprovide.lu` etc. if resolvable; Meluxina hostnames: login01/02/03.meluxina.luxprovide.lu? The standard entry is meluxina.luxprovide.lu. Specific nodes may not be SSH-reachable directly.)
> 3. Check if it's IP-based ban: try from a different network (phone hotspot) — if it works, the IP got throttled; wait for the ban window (often 10–30 min).
> 4. `ssh -v` to see how far it gets.
> 5. Check Meluxina status page / LuxProvide status announcements.
> 
> Also important: **reassure about the running training job.** Being logged out does NOT affect the batch job — it runs under SLURM on compute nodes independent of login sessions. Check status once reconnected: squeue. Also: the training is unaffected; checkpoints every 2000 steps; even node loss would leave resumable state (but a login logout doesn't touch it).
> 
> Also worth noting: the rapid-fire reconnects from VSCode auto-reconnect attempts after being logged out could worsen rate-limiting; advise pausing auto-reconnect briefly.
> 
> Keep it short and practical. No tools needed.

**Claude:**

Don't worry about the training first: **your job is unaffected.** It runs under SLURM on compute nodes, completely independent of login sessions — logout doesn't touch it, and checkpoints land every 2000 steps regardless.

The error itself — `kex_exchange_identification: Connection reset by peer` — happens *before* authentication: TCP connects, but the remote end drops the connection during the SSH banner exchange. On Meluxina this is almost always one of:

| Cause | Likelihood | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Connection rate-limiting / fail2ban on the login gateway** (rapid reconnects from VSCode's auto-retry after you were logged out can trigger it) | high | stop reconnecting for 5–10 min, then try once |
| **Login node busy or restarting** (meluxina load-balances across login01–03; a reset can be one sick node) | medium | just retry — you may land on a different node |
| **Your IP changed mid-session** (last login was from `45.66.41.127` — a VPN/proxy range); if you're roaming networks, the gateway may drop unfamiliar IPs | medium | try from the same network you used before, or a hotspot as a control |
| Cluster-side maintenance | low | check the LuxProvide status page / your email for announcements |

## What to do, in order

1. **Wait ~10 minutes without retrying** — reconnect storms extend bans.
2. Then a single verbose attempt:
   ```bash
   ssh -v -p 8822 <user>@meluxina.luxprovide.lu
   ```
   `-v` shows whether it dies at banner exchange (gateway issue) or gets further (auth issue).
3. If it still resets, try from a **different network** (phone hotspot). If that works, your usual IP is rate-limited — wait it out.
4. Check the [LuxProvide status page](https://docs.meluxina.luxprovide.lu/) or your mail for maintenance notices.

One practical note: if you use VSCode Remote-SSH, disable its auto-reconnect attempts until you're back in (each retry counts against the rate limit).

Once you're back in, verify the run in one command: `squeue -u $USER` (expect `cond_dplm2` still `R` on its node) and `grep "Validation Info" logs/slurm/cond_dplm2_<JOBID>.out | tail -3` — it should be past 50K steps by now, with `val/loss` continuing its slow decline toward the low-2.0s.

**Claude:**

> The user wants difficulty estimates for the remaining implementation stages before starting:
> 
> From the todo list:
> 1. CFG sampling in generate()
> 2. Function-recovery eval (InterProScan/DeepGO) + unconditional baseline
> 
> Let me think carefully about each based on everything we know about the codebase.
> 
> **Stage 1: CFG sampling**
> 
> Current state:
> - Training has CFG dropout: `AnnotationEmbedder` has `p_dropout_uncond` and a learnable null token per table. `force_unconditional=True` path exists and returns the null embedding for every sample.
> - `_encode_conditions(conditions, force_unconditional=False)` already supports the flag.
> - `generate()` (ConditionalDPLM2) stashes `self._active_layer_adapter_inputs` once, then delegates to parent's generate loop.
> 
> What CFG sampling requires at denoising step t:
> - Run model forward TWICE per step: once with conditional adapter inputs, once with unconditional (null) adapter inputs.
> - Combine logits: `logits = logits_uncond + w * (logits_cond - logits_uncond)`.
> - Then feed the combined logits into the parent's sampling machinery.
> 
> Difficulty: the parent's `generate` loop is inherited; we override `generate` in ConditionalDPLM2 already, but currently we just stash once and delegate. To do CFG we need to intervene at each denoising step BETWEEN forward and sampling. The parent's `generate` calls `self.forward_decoder(...)` which calls `self.forward(...)` and then samples. The sampling logic lives in `forward_decoder`.
> 
> Options:
> A. Override `forward_decoder` in ConditionalDPLM2: replicate the parent's 70-line forward_decoder but with two forward passes and logit combination. We deliberately avoided this before (brittleness), but it's a known 70-line body and we only need to modify the logits line. Alternatively:
> B. Cleaner trick: make `forward()` return combined logits during generation. I.e., stash BOTH conditional and unconditional adapter inputs; in `forward`, when in "CFG generation mode" (a flag), run the net twice (cond + uncond) and return `logits = uncond + w*(cond-uncond)` as `net_out["logits"]`. Then the parent's forward_decoder works unchanged! This is elegant: only `forward` gets a CFG branch, parent loop untouched. Cost: 2× compute per step (inherent to CFG).
>    - Implementation: `self._cfg_scale` + stash `_active_layer_adapter_inputs_uncond` (computed once with force_unconditional=True). In forward: if `_cfg_scale` set and stash present: run net with cond inputs → logits_c; run net with uncond inputs → logits_u; combine; return. ~25 lines in dplm2_conditional.py + CLI flags `--cfg-scale` (and maybe per-stage CFG ramp: CFP-Gen/other works often use constant w; keep constant w, optionally schedule later).
>    - API: `generate(..., cfg_scale=1.0)`; cfg_scale=1.0 → standard conditional (no extra pass needed; skip second forward); 0 → unconditional. Combine formula guidance.
>    - Testing: verify that w=1 equals current conditional path bit-wise-ish; w=0 equals --labels null path; both are 2-line checks using existing smoke scripts.
>    - Also expose in generate_conditional_dplm2.py CLI: `--cfg-scale` and a sweep mode maybe (loop over scales, separate dirs). Sweep mode = trivial loop.
> 
> Difficulty estimate: LOW-MEDIUM. ~1-2 hours including tests. The main risks: (1) double-forward doubles memory → batch size may need halving on 40GB A100 for seq len 512... but eval generation typically short sequences (128-256), fine. (2) interacting with bf16 autocast — both passes inside same autocast, fine. (3) The stash already holds cond inputs; add uncond stash.

Straightforward orchestration on top of generate_conditional_dplm2.py — a loop. LOW difficulty. But compute cost: e.g., 100 labels × 8 seqs × 128 len × (T=128 steps × 2 with CFG) — fine on 1 GPU, hours.

InterProScan run time: ~minutes-hours per 100 sequences (it scans against Panther etc. databases). Practical: install on login/head node CPU — MEDIUM operational, LOW coding.

Alternative cheap proxy: HMMER/Pfam — but labels are IPR/GO not Pfam... Actually IPR labels → InterProScan is the natural one. For GO: alternative is to map IPR→GO via InterPro2GO mapping (InterProScan output includes GO terms with -goterms flag!). So InterProScan alone can score BOTH IPR recovery AND GO-term recovery (via InterPro2GO association) — no DeepGO-SE needed for a first pass! That collapses (c) and (d) into one tool. **Claude:**

Fair ask — here's the honest breakdown, per stage, with the risks that actually bite.

## Stage 1 — CFG sampling in `generate()`: **LOW-MEDIUM, ~1–2 h**

The design is unusually clean because of how the conditioning is already wired:

- Training already does CFG dropout — `AnnotationEmbedder` has the learnable null token and a `force_unconditional=True` path. So the unconditional pass needs *no new model code*.
- The trick that keeps it small: instead of touching the parent's 70-line `forward_decoder`, extend the existing `forward()` override so that, when a `cfg_scale` is active, it runs the net **twice** (conditional + unconditional adapter inputs, both computed once and stashed) and returns `logits = uncond + w·(cond − uncond)` as ordinary logits. The parent's sampling machinery then consumes combined logits *unmodified*.
- Work: ~25 lines in `dplm2_conditional.py`, a `--cfg-scale` flag (plus an optional sweep loop) in `generate_conditional_dplm2.py`.
- Verification is cheap and decisive: `w=1.0` must reproduce today's conditional output, `w=0.0` must reproduce the `--labels null` output — both against existing runs.

Risks: 2× compute per denoising step (inherent to CFG; fine at eval lengths), and a subtle one — `w` sweeps interact with the noisy validation curve (aatype loss plateaued since 2K steps), so expect guidance to visibly change sequence character, but *fidelity* gains are an empirical question.

## Stage 2 — Function-recovery eval: **MEDIUM overall (~0.5–1 day), dominated by one operational piece**

| Sub-step | Difficulty | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 2a. Benchmark generation driver (per-label conditioned batches from CFP-Gen's held-out `test.pkl`) | **LOW** | Orchestration loop over `generate_conditional_dplm2.py`; the pkl is on disk, 8,309 seqs with labels |
| 2b. Unconditional baseline | **TRIVIAL** | `--labels null` already works |
| 2c. IPR recovery via InterProScan | **MEDIUM — the real cost is operational** | Installing InterProScan (Java + multi-GB databases) on Meluxina, then runtime: ~minutes-to-tens-of-minutes per 100 seqs. Coding is trivial: parse TSV, match predicted IPR accessions ∈ prompted set, sklearn F1/AUPR — CFP-Gen's `eval/eval_ipr.py` is directly adaptable |
| 2d. GO recovery | **Was HIGH with DeepGO-SE, but collapsible to LOW** | Key realization: InterProScan's `-goterms` flag emits GO terms via InterPro2GO mapping — so **one tool scores both IPR and GO recovery**, no DeepGO-SE install. Caveat to document: this is domain-mapping GO, not DeepGO-SE's learned predictor — a defensible first pass, not the CFP-Gen-identical protocol |
| 2e. Metrics: MRR, MMD (k-mer spectrum), F1/AUPR | **LOW** | Mechanical port from `cfpgen/eval/metrics/` |
| 2f. Positive/negative controls | **LOW** | Positive control = InterProScan on the real `test.pkl` sequences (predictor ceiling); negative = the unconditional baseline |

**Main risks, ranked:** (1) InterProScan installation friction — the one piece I'd budget slack for; (2) protocol decisions that sound boring but change numbers — match thresholds, whether to score all prompted labels or the primary one, downsampling; (3) GPU contention is *not* a risk — generation jobs can run on `test`/`short` QOS concurrently with the training job on `long` (different QOS, `MaxJobs=1` is per-QOS).

## Recommended order

1. **CFG now** (1–2 h) — the trained model's 10% dropout is currently unused at inference; this is the highest-leverage knob for eval and it's cheap.
2. **Eval scaffolding while training finishes** (~15 h left): 2a + 2b + 2e first (pure code, no new deps, testable against the *existing* 200-step checkpoint locally), then InterProScan install + 2c/2d as the operational piece.
3. When training lands (~tomorrow evening): generate at scale with a CFG sweep, run InterProScan, first results table.

> **Established GO evaluation landscape:**
> 1. CAFA-standard: Fmax (protein-centric, threshold-free max F1 over precision-recall) + Smin (semantic distance weighting errors by ontology distance). Implementations to port: CAFA-evaluator (BioComputingUP; pip-installable python, handles GO hierarchy propagation — "hierarchical concept dependencies"), deepgo2's evaldfdf scripts.
> 2. Predictor-based GO recovery (CFP-Gen protocol): run predictor on generated seqs, compare predicted terms vs prompted terms: micro/macro F1, AUPR, AUC + MRR/MMD.
> 3. Predictor options for GO recovery:
>    - DeepGO-SE: SOTA-ish sequence GO predictor (Nature MI 2024), MFO Fmax 0.386 on their benchmark (beats NetGO3, DeepGOPlus, TALE). Uses pretrained protein LLM + approximate semantic reasoning over GO. Per-branch models (MFO/BPO/CCO). Outputs per-term probabilities over the full branch term set → threshold-free curves possible (Fmax directly!) rather than single-threshold matching. Benefits: established, CFP-Gen-compatible (their eval_go.py parses its output), per-term probabilities enable Fmax/AUPR rather than brittle thresholds. Costs: separate research stack (deepgo2 repo, pretrained checkpoints, data files GO.txt/definitions), runs ESM embeddings per sequence (GPU/CPU minutes), license/checkpoint hosting quirks.
>    - NetGO 3.0: web server primarily; bit harder to run locally at scale.
>    - DeepGOPlus: simpler (CNN+DIAMOND alignment), easy install, but weaker.
>    - InterProScan -goterms: not a learned GO predictor — GO via InterPro2GO mapping; cheap, already needed for IPR; biased toward domain-bearing regions; single-threshold (no probabilities) → can't do Fmax curves, only set-match at "whatever IPS reports".

## Research walkthrough — GO/IPR function metrics

**The established standard is CAFA's protocol.** The protein-function-prediction community (CAFA challenges) evaluates with two protein-centric metrics ([CAFA3 report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6864930/)):

- **Fmax** — max F1 over per-term prediction thresholds (precision-recall curve, threshold-free)
- **Smin** — minimum semantic distance: weights a wrong GO prediction by how far it sits from the truth in the ontology graph (respects GO's hierarchy)

There's a ready-to-port implementation: [CAFA-evaluator (BioComputingUP)](https://github.com/BioComputingUP/CAFA-evaluator) — open-source Python, GO-hierarchy-aware, computes Fmax/Smin/PR-curves. **Key dependency: it needs per-term probabilities from a predictor**, not binary predictions.

That's where the GO-predictor choice matters:

| Predictor | What it gives you | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| **DeepGO-SE** ([Nature MI 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-024-00795-w), [code](https://github.com/bio-ontology-research-group/deepgo2)) | Per-term **probabilities** over full GO branches (MFO/BPO/CCO) → enables the CAFA **Fmax/Smin** protocol properly. SOTA-class: MFO Fmax 0.386, beating NetGO3 / DeepGOPlus / TALE. Uses protein-LLM embeddings + semantic reasoning over GO. **Also the exact predictor CFP-Gen used for GO recovery** — so its output format already has an eval parser in `cfpgen/eval/` | Separate research stack: deepgo2 repo, pretrained checkpoints, GO data files; per-sequence embedding pass (CPU/GPU minutes) |
| **InterProScan `-goterms`** | GO terms via InterPro2GO mapping — free alongside the IPR recovery you already decided on | **No probabilities** → only single-threshold set-match, no Fmax curves; GO comes from domain co-annotation, a weaker proxy than a learned predictor |
| NetGO3 / DeepGOPlus / TALE | Established baselines | Web-server-first or older methods; DeepGO-SE beats them in its own benchmark and is the one with a CFP-Gen-compatible output parser |

**My recommendation:** InterProScan for IPR recovery now (decided), **plus DeepGO-SE for GO scoring** — because (a) your professors asked for *established* GO metrics, and Fmax/Smin via CAFA-evaluator is exactly that, (b) CFP-Gen comparability comes free, and (c) the loss-delta proxy alone won't show *generation* fidelity. The Smin semantic-distance metric is a particularly good story for us: it rewards predictions that are *ontologically near* the prompt — a gentler bar than exact match, appropriate for a first-generation conditional model.

Also worth knowing: the **loss-delta proxy doesn't require restarting training from scratch** — we can resume from `last.ckpt` (optimizer + step state restore) with the new validation hook, costing ~10 minutes of downtime and giving you the function-sensitivity curve for the remaining 50K steps plus a checkpoint-sweep backwards over already-saved checkpoints.

Sources: [CAFA3 report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6864930/) · [CAFA-evaluator](https://github.com/BioComputingUP/CAFA-evaluator) · [DeepGO-SE paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-024-00795-w) · [deepgo2 code](https://github.com/bio-ontology-research-group/deepgo2) · [Expanded evaluation (Genome Biology)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13059-016-1037-6) · [NetGO 3.0](https://dmiip.sjtu.edu.cn/ng3.0/)

> 2. **Why sampling from p(x|c) alone underuses the training signal.** During training with CFG dropout, the model sees both p(x|c) and p(x). The difference term (log p(x|c) − log p(x|∅)) is exactly the *evidence that the condition provides* — the marginal effect of the labels. With w=1 you get exactly p(x|c) (vanilla); with w>1 you extrapolate away from the marginal, amplifying whatever conditional signal exists.
> 
> 3. **Why it matters SPECIFICALLY for adapter training at frozen base.** The adapter's total influence on the 650M-parameter frozen computation is a 19.5M-parameter residual. It's a small lever. The measured effect exists (loss differs, val loss dropped), but the *sampling-time* effect per denoising step may be modest relative to the base model's strong prior (which predicts aa from struct context very well). Empirically across the literature (guidance in discrete diffusion: SEDD, DPLM itself has guidance experiments?, RDM, and in continuous diffusion universally), w in the 1.5–4 range is typically needed to get strong condition adherence, and papers evaluate a sweep.

**Claude:**

Your understanding of the data flow is exactly right — and your question is legitimate: **vanilla conditional generation already works, and CFG is not required for it.** Let me answer both parts precisely.

## The data flow (confirming your picture)

At each denoising step, the noisy sequence `x_t = [struct | aa]` embeds and flows through the 33 frozen layers. At each layer, the hidden states `h` (which carry the sequence information) are fed to the parallel adapters along with the condition: `Δ(h, s)` where `s = ProjectionMLP(Embed(GO, IPR))` depends **only on the labels**, and the output is summed into the residual stream:

```
h' = h + Δ_ipr(h, s_ipr) + Δ_go(h, s_go)
```

So yes: sequence flows through the base path, condition enters only via the adapters, and the adapters see the sequence. Sampling from this model *is* conditional generation — nothing is missing mechanically.

## So why CFG?

Because vanilla sampling answers a slightly different question than the one we're asked. Vanilla draws from the model's learned p̂(x|c). CFG draws from a *sharpened* distribution built from the model's own two learned densities:

```
log p_w(x|c) ∝ log p̂(x|∅) + w · ( log p̂(x|c) − log p̂(x|∅) )
```

The term `(log p̂(x|c) − log p̂(x|∅))` is the **marginal evidence the labels provide** — the per-step, per-position difference the condition makes relative to no condition. Three reasons this matters for us specifically:

1. **Likelihood training doesn't optimize conditional *distinguishability*.** The diffusion loss is satisfied if the labels shift log-probabilities by a modest amount — the base model already predicts amino acids well from structural context, so "ignoring" the condition costs the training loss very little. This is the classic **condition-ignoring** failure mode (it's listed as a named risk in our own [conditional_dplm_pfam.md](plans/conditional_dplm_pfam.md)). The adapter is a 19.5M-parameter residual pushing on a frozen 650M computation — a small lever by design. CFG amplifies that small per-step lever by `w`, and the amplification compounds across ~T denoising steps.

2. **Typicality/mode collapse toward the base prior.** A broad GO label's conditional distribution is a mixture over many protein families. Un-guided sampling tends to fall back to high-prior "generic protein" modes where the frozen base is most confident. The extrapolation term pushes sampling toward the condition-specific mode instead.

3. **CFG is also the diagnostic instrument, not just a quality knob.** This is the part that matters most for the professors' point 4. If we evaluate vanilla-conditional sampling and function recovery is mediocre, we *cannot distinguish* "the adapters learned nothing" from "the adapters learned something that vanilla sampling under-expresses." A guidance sweep (w = 1, 2, 4, 8) deconvolves the two: recovery rising then falling with w → signal exists, and w becomes a reported trade-off; recovery flat in w → the conditioning genuinely failed. That dose-response curve is the strongest evidence available that the function modality is (or isn't) being used.

Two honest caveats:

- **w > 1 trades diversity for adherence.** At high guidance, samples homogenize and can degenerate — universal in diffusion, and we'll see it in the sweep. That's why evaluation reports a sweep rather than one w.
- **The alternative is classifier guidance** (a separately trained sequence→function classifier steering sampling), which is what your professors' future-steps line also mentions. CFG is the cheap version: no classifier to train — it reuses the model's own null-conditioned head, which exists *because* we trained with the 10% CFG dropout. That dropout was the down-payment; the sampling-time combination is how we collect it. (CFP-Gen does exactly this — their `FuncTagEmbedder` has the same +1 null embedding for the same reason.)

## Bottom line

Nothing is blocking vanilla conditional generation — we'll use it as the **w = 1.0** anchor of the sweep. CFG adds ~25 lines (a second forward pass per step with the null-condition adapter inputs, then logit combination) and turns the evaluation from a single point into a dose-response curve: it's simultaneously the fidelity knob and the cleanest evidence for whether the function modality learned anything at all. That's why it's queued before the eval stack — want me to go ahead with it now?

|---|---|---|
| **InterProScan** (EMBL-EBI) | IPR recovery on generated sequences; `--goterms` also gives a GO proxy | Java tool + ~5–10 GB of databases; CPU only; the heaviest install |
| **DeepGO-SE** ([deepgo2 repo](https://github.com/bio-ontology-research-group/deepgo2)) | Per-term GO probabilities → the CAFA **Fmax/Smin** protocol; CFP-Gen's exact GO predictor (so `eval_go.py` parses it natively) | Repo + pretrained branch checkpoints (MFO/BPO/CCO); per-sequence LLM-embedding pass |
| **CAFA-evaluator** ([BioComputingUP](https://github.com/BioComputingUP/CAFA-evaluator)) | Fmax/Smin with GO-hierarchy propagation | Python, pip-level — trivial |
| **go.obo** | GO ontology graph — needed by DeepGO-SE, CAFA-evaluator, and `eval_go.py`'s ancestor expansion | ~40 MB download from geneontology.org — currently **missing on disk** |

## The protocol these feed

Four arms × the same predictors → one table:

| Arm | Model | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| Ours | `step_99999.ckpt` | held-out GO+IPR prompts (+ CFG sweep) |
| Ours-null | `step_99999.ckpt` | null condition |
| Vanilla | pretrained DPLM-2 650M | unconditional |
| Positive control | — | real `test.pkl` sequences |

Metrics: IPR set-match F1/AUPR (CFP-Gen protocol), GO Fmax/Smin (CAFA protocol), MRR/MMD distribution metrics.

## Recommendation first: keep predictors **out** of the Docker image

Three reasons: they're CPU-only (no point shipping them in the CUDA image), InterProScan's databases would balloon the image by ~10 GB, and DeepGO-SE needs its own Python env that would fight the pinned `dplm` dependencies. The clean protocol is a **file handoff**: GPU container generates FASTAs → predictors run on the *host* with their own environments → scorer (inside the container, since it imports `byprot`) computes the table. The plain-directory sandbox has nothing to do with it.

## 1. InterProScan — host install, CPU allocation

```bash
# on a login node — tools live on $PROJECT
mkdir -p $PROJECT/tools && cd $PROJECT/tools

# latest 5.x from the EBI FTP (check https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/software/unix/iprscan/5/ for current version)
wget https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/software/unix/iprscan/5/5.68-99.0/interproscan-5.68-99.0-64-bit.tar.gz
tar -xzf interproscan-5.68-99.0-64-bit.tar.gz
cd interproscan-5.68-99.0

# needs Java 11+ — Meluxina has modules:
module spider Java          # find the exact module name
module load Java/XX         # e.g. Java/17

# smoke test (bundled test data):
./interproscan.sh -i test_proteins.fasta -f TSV -goterms --disable-precalc -T ./tmp
```

Run it on an **CPU allocation**, not the login node (it's multithreaded and wants RAM):

```bash
salloc --account=p201418 -p cpu --qos=short --cpus-per-task=16 --mem=32G -t 02:00:00
# then inside:
module load Java/XX
IPS=$PROJECT/tools/interproscan-5.68-99.0/interproscan.sh
$IPS -i $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_cond/aatype.fasta \
     -f TSV -goterms --disable-precalc \
     -o $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_cond/ips.tsv \
     -T $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_cond/ips_tmp -cpu 16
# repeat per arm: ours_null, vanilla, real
```

~800 sequences should take minutes-to-tens-of-minutes at 16 threads. If Java isn't available as a module, the fallback is installing OpenJDK into `$PROJECT/tools` (tarball from adoptium.net, no root needed — just `export PATH=$PROJECT/tools/jdk-17/bin:$PATH`).

## 2. DeepGO-SE — separate conda env on `$PROJECT`

```bash
cd $PROJECT/tools
git clone https://github.com/bio-ontology-research-group/deepgo2.git
cd deepgo2

conda create -n deepgose python=3.9 -y
conda activate deepgose
pip install -r requirements.txt    # torch CPU is fine; transformers, etc.

# Data + pretrained weights: follow the repo README's data section — it
# downloads the GO ontology, the deepgo2-format datasets, and the trained
# DeepGO-SE model files per branch. One step I can't specify from memory is
# the exact Zenodo/URL of the weights, so check the README's "Data" section.
```

The one environment-specific thing: the `predict` entrypoint signature. That's why [`predictors.py`](src/byprot/eval/predictors.py#L70) takes `deepgose_dir` / `python_bin` / `weights_dir` as arguments — once you know the exact invocation from the checkout you cloned, either call it directly or fix the argument order in the hook. The **TSV parser is already done and tested**, and it's the piece that matters for scoring.

Smoke test the predictor:

```bash
conda activate deepgose
python predict.py mfo $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_cond/aatype.fasta \
    /tmp/dg_test.tsv <weights-dir>     # verify arg order against the repo
head /tmp/dg_test.tsv                 # expect: seq_id \t GO:XXXXXXX \t score
```

## 3. go.obo — 40 MB, needed by three components

```bash
wget https://geneontology.org/ontology/go.obo -O $PROJECT/tools/go.obo
```

## 4. The full workflow, end to end

```bash
# --- 1. GENERATE (GPU allocation, inside container — as before) ---
cd $PROJECT/dplm-repo
sbatch scripts/eval_function/...        # or interactive; per-arm FASTAs land in eval_runs/

# --- 2. INTERPROSCAN (CPU allocation, host Java) ---
for arm in ours_cond ours_null vanilla real; do
  $IPS -i eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/aatype.fasta -f TSV -goterms \
       --disable-precalc -o eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/ips.tsv -T ... -cpu 16
done

# --- 3. DEEPGO-SE (deepgose conda env, CPU) ---
for arm in ours_cond ours_null vanilla real; do
  conda activate deepgose
  python predict.py mfo eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/aatype.fasta \
      eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/deepgose.tsv <weights>
done

# --- 4. SCORE (inside the dplm container — needs byprot) ---
apptainer exec ... python scripts/eval_function/score_function_eval.py \
  --evaldir eval_runs/fn_eval_v1 \
  --arms ours_cond,ours_null,vanilla \
  --ips-tsv ours_cond=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_cond/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv ours_null=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_null/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv vanilla=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/vanilla/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv real=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/real/ips.tsv \
  --deepgose-tsv <same pattern per arm> \
  --obo $PROJECT/tools/go.obo
# → eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/results.md  (the comparison table)
```

## Locally (no Meluxina needed for setup)

Both installs work the same way in `$HOME` or anywhere — InterProScan just needs a JDK (likely already present via conda: `conda install -c conda-forge openjdk`), and DeepGO-SE gets its own conda env. The scorer runs in your existing `dplm` conda env (it only needs numpy/sklearn + byprot). So you can validate the whole predictor path locally on a few dozen sequences before committing Meluxina allocations.

One flag: the **arg-order of the deepgose `predict` call** and the **weight-file names** are the two things I can't guarantee from memory — budget 30 minutes of README-reading when you clone it, and everything downstream (parser → CAFA-evaluator-style scoring) is already wired.

## Why it's refusing, and one thing to try

A 145 ms connection *refusal* (not timeout) from both a datacenter IP and your network looks like **deliberate IP-range blocking** by EBI — possibly anti-scraping. Your last Meluxina login came from `45.66.41.127`, a VPN range. **If your VPN is on, turn it off and retry `curl -v https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/`** — direct home connections are frequently not blocked when VPN/datacenter ranges are.

If it works without VPN, you have two paths reopened: the IPS 5.78 FTP download, and the IPS 6 nextflow pipeline (`nextflow run ... -resume` after `curl` succeeds — or manually place the downloaded `interpro-latest.tar.gz` where the `DOWNLOAD_INTERPRO` process expects it).

## Priority note

Don't sink time into IPS 6 right now — it needs the same unreachable FTP, and IPS 5.78 from GitHub unblocks the eval immediately with everything the scorer consumes (`ips.tsv` with IPR accessions + GO terms). IPS 6 is a nice-to-have upgrade, not a requirement; our parser and metrics are version-agnostic.

Also keep in mind the disk cost before extracting: 6.6 GB tarball + ~15 GB extracted — check `df -h /home/cherry` first.

## Step 0 — pull the scripts

```bash
cd $PROJECT/dplm-repo
git pull origin main
ls scripts/eval_function/    # expect: generate_eval_set.py score_function_eval.py check_function_metrics.py
```

## Step 1 — generate the eval set (GPU allocation, in container)

Start with a pilot to validate end-to-end, then scale:

```bash
export DPLM_SIF=$PROJECT/dplm_sandbox
unset DPLM_SIF   # only if you want the auto-discovery instead
scripts/meluxina/interactive.sh alloc

# --- inside the HOST shell (allocation alive): ---
source scripts/meluxina/common.sh
run_in_container "${DPLM_PY}" scripts/eval_function/generate_eval_set.py \
  --ckpt $PROJECT/dplm-logs/cond_dplm2_650m_cfpgen/checkpoints/step_99999.0-loss_1.95.ckpt \
  --n-labels 8 --seqs-per-label 4 --len 128 \
  --arms ours_cond,ours_null,vanilla,real \
  --out $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_pilot
```

Pilot throughput: ~4 labels × ~1.5 s/label-batch per arm — a few minutes. Verify: `ls $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_pilot/*/aatype.fasta` (4 files) and `head` a couple of sequences (should be AA strings, no masks).

If good, run the **full set** (~45–90 min for all arms; use a `short` allocation for the 6h wall):

```bash
run_in_container "${DPLM_PY}" scripts/eval_function/generate_eval_set.py \
  --ckpt $PROJECT/dplm-logs/cond_dplm2_650m_cfpgen/checkpoints/step_99999.0-loss_1.95.ckpt \
  --n-labels 32 --seqs-per-label 8 --len 256 --cfg-scale 1.0 \
  --arms ours_cond,ours_null,vanilla,real \
  --out $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1
```

(Optionally also a CFG-sweep variant — `--cfg-sweep 1,4` produces `ours_cond` rows per w; add later once the base table exists.)

## Step 2 — InterProScan on the FASTAs (CPU allocation, host-side)

Exit the container first (`exit` back to the host shell, or fresh login):

```bash
module spider Java     # find the exact module name/version
module load Java/<ver> # IPS 5.78 wants Java 11+
IPS=$PROJECT/tools/interproscan-5.78-109.0/interproscan.sh

# one-time smoke test on IPS's own bundled test data:
cd $PROJECT/tools/interproscan-5.78-109.0
./interproscan.sh -i test_proteins.fasta -f TSV -goterms --disable-precalc -T ./tmp
head test_proteins.fasta.tsv    # expect tab-separated annotations

# then the real run — CPU allocation:
salloc --account=p201418 -p cpu --qos=short --cpus-per-task=16 --mem=32G -t 02:00:00
for arm in ours_cond ours_null vanilla real; do
  $IPS -i $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/aatype.fasta \
       -f TSV -goterms --disable-precalc \
       -o $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/ips.tsv \
       -T $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/ips_tmp -cpu 16
  wc -l $PROJECT/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/ips.tsv   # expect >0
done
```

~2K sequences at 16 threads: minutes to tens of minutes total.

> 
> ## 4. Metric primer — what each metric measures
> 
> ### 4.1 MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) — *sequence modality, label-conditionality*
> 
> - **Measures:** whether sequences generated *for* a label are recognizable as members of that label's family — i.e., condition-sensitivity of the sequence distribution. For every prompted label L, the mean k-mer spectrum embedding of its generated group is ranked among the mean embeddings of all reference (real) label-groups by MMD distance; the reciprocal of L's rank is averaged over labels.
> - **Modality / data:** sequence strings only (no predictor). Generated FASTA + real held-out FASTA + per-sequence label sets from the manifest.
> - **Range/reading:** 1.0 = every generated group is closest to its own real group; ~1/n_labels = random. Higher is better.
> - **Cannot tell you:** whether the sequences would actually *function* — it measures distributional proximity in k-mer space, not annotation fidelity.
> 
> ### 4.2 MMD (Maximum Mean Discrepancy) — *sequence modality, distributional fidelity*
> 
> - **Measures:** distance between the generated sequence distribution and the real distribution in k-mer spectrum space. Linear kernel: Euclidean distance between mean embeddings. Gaussian kernel: full kernel two-sample statistic with median-heuristic bandwidth — sensitive to higher-order composition differences.
> - **Modality / data:** sequence strings only; generated arm vs the real arm.
> - **Range/reading:** 0 = indistinguishable distributions; lower is better. Interpret relative to the real arm's self-MMD (noise floor).
> - **Caveat:** MMD≈0 means "protein-like overall composition", not "the right protein" — it is condition-blind unless compared per-label.
> 
> ### 4.3 IPR set-match (InterProScan recovery) — *function modality*
> 
> - **Measures:** whether the generated sequences, when annotated by InterProScan, recover the IPR domains they were conditioned on. Per sequence: predicted IPR accessions (predictor output) vs prompted IPR set (held-out ground truth) → multi-label precision/recall/F1 (micro + macro), AUPR, AUC over the binarized label matrix.
> - **Modality / data:** generated sequences → InterProScan (external predictor) → IPR accession sets; ground truth = prompt labels from the manifest.
> - **Range/reading:** F1 in [0,1], higher better. Micro weights frequent domains; macro treats rare domains equally — report both.
> - **Caveat:** scores are bounded by InterProScan's own recall on natural proteins — that's why the real arm (positive control) is scored identically: it defines the predictor ceiling.
> 
> ### 4.4 GO set-match (DeepGO-SE recovery, thresholded) — *function modality*
> 
> - **Measures:** same recovery idea for GO terms: DeepGO-SE assigns per-term probabilities to each generated sequence; terms with score ≥ 0.5 form the predicted set, compared to the prompted GO set (ancestor-expanded so that predicting a child of a true term is credited partially... actually ancestor expansion expands GT with ancestors; predicting an ancestor of a true term is counted correct since ancestors of GT terms are included in GT).
> - **Modality / data:** generated sequences → DeepGO-SE → per-term probabilities; GT = prompted GO-F terms expanded over the GO DAG (go.obo).
> - **Reading:** F1/AUPR as above; the ancestor expansion prevents penalizing semantically-near predictions.
> 
> ### 4.5 GO Fmax (CAFA protein-centric) — *function modality, threshold-free*
> 
> - **Measures:** the CAFA-standard maximum F1: sweep a score threshold over DeepGO-SE's per-term probabilities, compute per-protein precision/recall at each threshold (proteins with no prediction and no truth excluded), average, and take the maximum over thresholds.
> - **Modality / data:** DeepGO-SE probability matrix vs ancestor-expanded GO ground truth.
> - **Range/reading:** [0,1], higher better; 0.386 was DeepGO-SE's SOTA MFO value on its own benchmark — a useful external calibration point: our generated sequences will sit below the natural-protein ceiling.
> - **Why it's the headline GO metric:** threshold-free (no arbitrary 0.5), community-standard (CAFA), and sensitive to ranking quality, not just coverage.
> 
> ### 4.6 Smin (deferred) — *function modality, semantic distance*
> 
> - **Measures:** minimum semantic distance between predicted and true GO sets, weighting errors by information content (how deep/specific terms are in the DAG). Computed by the CAFA-evaluator tool on the same inputs as Fmax. Lower is better. Deferred: requires information-accumulation weights over the full GO corpus.
> 
> ### 4.7 Structural metrics (degradation check, queued) — *structure modality*
> 
> - For the "does function training degrade the pretrained model?" question: **designability** (fraction of co-generated structures with ESMFold self-consistency scTM ≥ 0.5), **pLDDT** (per-residue confidence), **diversity** (mean pairwise scTM / Foldseek cluster count), and **forward-folding TM-score** on CAMEO 2022. Data: co-generated struct tokens → decoded PDBs → ESMFold/TMscore. Identical-settings comparison: pretrained DPLM-2 vs our checkpoint under null conditions.
> 
> ### 4.8 Training/validation losses (logged curves) — *both modalities*
> 
> - **val/loss** — the DPLM-2 denoising objective: label-smoothed cross-entropy on the noised tokens, weighted by diffusion timestep, summed over the struct and aa tracks. This is the quantity that must not degrade.
> - **val/aatype_loss** — the aa-track component; **val/struct_loss** — the struct-track component. During adapter training the aa component plateaued early while the struct component kept improving — the adapters modulate shared hidden states, so conditioning also (mildly) helps structure denoising.
> - **val/*_index_accuracy** — fraction of noised positions whose argmax prediction matches the target token (per modality). 0.11 aa accuracy is against the full 8229-token vocab at mixed noise levels, not a 20-way classification.
>

## How the CFP-Gen arm works without integration

[scripts/eval_function/cfpgen_arm.py](scripts/eval_function/cfpgen_arm.py) is a **standalone script run from inside the cfpgen repo** — CFP-Gen forks the entire `byprot` package, so its model class (`byprot.models.lm.cfp_gen`) can only be imported with the cfpgen checkout first on `sys.path`. Running it as its own process with `PYTHONPATH=<cfpgen-repo>` sidesteps the collision entirely. It:

1. Reads `<evaldir>/manifest.json` — the *same* held-out prompts our arms used (CFP-Gen's label-ID space is identical, since our mapping pkls came from their repo)
2. Loads `CondDiffusionProteinLanguageModel.from_pretrained(ckpt)` — your local `cfpgen_650m/checkpoints/last.ckpt` works as-is
3. Generates with their native API (`go_label`/`ipr_label` tensors, their sampler, partial-mask convention)
4. Writes `cfpgen/aatype.fasta` + registers itself in the manifest → the scorer picks it up as any other arm, **same prompts, same predictor TSVs, same metrics**

Documented deviations (in the docstring): fixed length 256 (they sample 200–400 — fixed keeps MMD/MRR comparable across arms) and no motif conditioning (this is the "w/ GO and IPR" ablation row, the closest comparable variant).

**Run command** (from the cfpgen checkout, any env with torch — their fork or dplm's conda env works since the path shadowing handles imports):

```bash
cd /home/cherry/dev/phd/cfpgen
PYTHONPATH=/home/cherry/dev/phd/cfpgen python \
  /home/cherry/dev/phd/dplm/scripts/eval_function/cfpgen_arm.py \
  --evaldir eval_runs/fn_eval_v1 \
  --ckpt cfpgen_650m/checkpoints/last.ckpt
```

And the paper-numbers fallback also stands: CFP-Gen's Tab 1 rows (their `w/ GO and IPR` variant) are quotable as a reference band, with the caveat that our label subsample differs — the independent-arm run gives the strictly comparable version.

**Key realization:** of all the metrics we promised, **only the two GO columns (GO set-match + GO Fmax) are truly gated on DeepGO-SE**. InterProScan alone unblocks MRR, MMD, *and* IPR recovery — and via `-goterms` it even gives a threshold-free-proxy GO set-match. So a meaningful results table (ours_cond vs ours_null vs vanilla, IPR recovery + distribution metrics) can be produced **without DeepGO-SE**.

## Step 1 — get InterProScan running (no blockers)

```bash
cd /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools
tar -xzf interproscan-5.78-109.0-64-bit.tar.gz     # 6.6 GB → ~15 GB; takes a few minutes
cd interproscan-5.78-109.0

# Java 11+ (if not already installed from the earlier step):
conda install -c conda-forge openjdk=17 -y

# First run self-initializes the bundled databases (long — 10-30 min, one-time).
# Point its temp dir somewhere with space:
./interproscan.sh -i /dev/null -f TSV -goterms --disable-precalc -T /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/ips_tmp 2>&1 | head -5
```

Then generate the eval set (small pilot first) and run IPS on the arms:

```bash
cd /home/cherry/dev/phd/dplm
source /home/cherry/miniconda/bin/activate dplm
python scripts/eval_function/generate_eval_set.py \
  --ckpt logs/cond_dplm2_650m_cfpgen/checkpoints/step_99999.0-loss_1.95.ckpt \
  --n-labels 8 --seqs-per-label 4 --len 128 \
  --arms ours_cond,ours_null,vanilla,real \
  --out eval_runs/fn_eval_v1

IPS=/home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/interproscan-5.78-109.0/interproscan.sh
for arm in ours_cond ours_null vanilla real; do
  $IPS -i eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/aatype.fasta -f TSV -goterms \
       --disable-precalc -o eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/ips.tsv \
       -T /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/ips_tmp -cpu 8
done

# score immediately — IPS-only, no DeepGO-SE needed:
python scripts/eval_function/score_function_eval.py \
  --evaldir eval_runs/fn_eval_v1 --arms ours_cond,ours_null,vanilla \
  --ips-tsv ours_cond=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_cond/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv ours_null=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_null/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv vanilla=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/vanilla/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv real=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/real/ips.tsv \
  --obo /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/go.obo
```

(Grab go.obo locally too: `wget https://geneontology.org/ontology/go.obo -O /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/go.obo`.)

That yields the **first real results table**: MRR, MMD, and IPR set-match for ours_cond vs ours_null vs vanilla vs real-ceiling — the core of the professors' point 4.

4. **Meanwhile**: InterProScan `-goterms` gives GO *set-match* (thresholded, no Fmax) for free — so even a prolonged DeepGO-SE outage only costs us the Fmax column, not the whole GO story.

> 
> The important analysis for our evaluation:
> 
> **What changes between InterPro releases 101 → 109 → (v6's InterPro release):**
> - New IPR accessions added; some merged/retired
> - Member database HMMs updated (PANTHER, CDD, Gene3D, etc.) → borderline HMMER hits shift
> - InterPro2GO mappings updated → GO terms per entry change
> - IPS 6 also adds new analyses/architecture
> 
> **Impact on OUR metrics:**

CFP-Gen's prompts are InterPro-101-era annotations; if release 109 retired/merged some of those accessions, IPS 109 can never output them → systematic recall dip for those labels in ALL arms equally. > - The `set_match_metrics` operates on prompted accessions vs predicted accessions — version-difference affects which can appear.

> - Optionally check prompt-accession coverage after the first real-arm IPS run.

Same sequence can get different match sets at the margins. Identical only if the member DBs and InterPro release were identical — they aren't.

> **Comparability with older papers using v5**: standard practice in the field is that InterProScan versions differ across papers; most papers don't even pin it. Our design (same predictor for all arms + positive control ceiling) makes version mismatch a minor caveat, not a validity threat. The one thing to avoid: mixing versions ACROSS arms — which our design already prevents.

**Claude:**

## Answers to your three questions

### 1. What did CFP-Gen use? (found, hardcoded in their code)

`eval_ipr.py:49-60` pins it exactly:

- **InterProScan 5.69-101.0** — i.e. **InterPro release 101** (the second number in the IPS version *is* the InterPro release)
- **Java 11** (`jdk-11.0.24`)
- **High-throughput mode** (`-dp`), TSV output, `-goterms`, 32 CPUs

Our downloaded version is **5.78-109.0** → InterPro release **109** — same major pipeline, **8 InterPro releases newer**.

### 2. Should we use InterProScan 6?

**No — not for the comparison run.** IPS 6 (6.0.x) is the *furthest* from CFP-Gen's stack: new nextflow architecture, newer member-database versions, and it also depends on the currently-unreachable EBI FTP for its databases (your nextflow failure). Practical, too: your 5.78 install works today.

### 3. Are v5.78-109 vs v6 numbers identical? Comparable with v5-era papers?

**Not identical, and not expected to be.** Between InterPro 101 → 109 → the v6-era release, three things drift:

1. **Member-database HMMs update** (PANTHER, CDD, Gene3D, …) — borderline HMMER hits shift, so the same sequence can gain/lose signature matches.
2. **The InterPro accession space changes** — new entries added, some merged/retired. An accession CFP-Gen prompted with (InterPro-101 era) that release 109 merged away can never appear in our predictions.
3. **InterPro2GO mappings update** — GO terms attached to entries change, affecting `-goterms` output.

Most strong matches are stable across versions — but the *margins* move, and set-match metrics are exactly at the margins.

### What this actually means for our evaluation — the key point

**Our design already controls for this.** Every arm — `ours_cond`, `ours_null`, `vanilla`, `cfpgen`, `real` — is scored with the *same* InterProScan install. The arm-to-arm comparison (the professors' point 4) is internally consistent regardless of version. Matching CFP-Gen's 5.69-101.0 would only matter for reproducing their *published absolute* numbers — and even then, we'd re-score CFP-Gen's outputs with our install anyway, which is the stronger design.

**Recommended:** run the main table with **5.78-109.0** for all arms (downloaded, working, done). Record the version in the results caption. Two follow-ups, both cheap:

1. **Coverage check after the first real-arm IPS run** — what fraction of prompted IPR accessions appear anywhere in the output? If high (>90%), version drift is a non-issue in practice; if some prompted accessions never appear (retired in 101→109), note that those labels are systematically capped — equally in all arms, so the comparison survives.
2. **Exact-version CFP-Gen replication is possible later** if a reviewer asks: the [5.69-101.0 release exists on GitHub](https://github.com/ebi-pf-team/interproscan/releases/tag/5.69-101.0) (5.5 GB, md5 `e5ba8154...`) but the tarball is hosted on the same EBI FTP that's currently blocking us — so it's gated on EBI connectivity returning (or the VPN-off retry).

Decision recorded in [plans/meetings.md](plans/meetings.md) §4. Practical next step unchanged: run the IPS smoke on `test_proteins.fasta`, then the eval-set generation + per-arm IPS, and paste the coverage number with the first results table.

The run is *almost* clean — three of four IPS runs succeeded (`ours_cond`, `vanilla`, `real` all completed). The failure is real and interesting:

## Root cause

The `ours_null` arm contains a sequence with **`-` and `.` characters** — gap tokens from the DPLM-2 vocabulary (ids 29/30) that the diffusion model sampled as actual output. InterProScan's protein validator rejects any non-standard residue, so the whole arm's load fails. **Claude:**

Pushed (`e7bdb3d`). Here's what happened and the recovery path:

## Root cause

The `ours_null` arm contained a sequence with **gap tokens** (`-` and `.` — legitimate DPLM-2 vocabulary entries, ids 30/29) that the null-conditioned model sampled as output. InterProScan's protein validator rejects any non-standard residue and kills the entire file load. The telling detail: `ours_cond`, `vanilla`, and `real` all passed — the **null-conditioned model is the noisiest sampler**, which is itself a small data point (it drifts toward the base prior with composition artifacts when unguided).

## Fixes (committed)

1. **Sanitization at FASTA-write time** in both generation drivers: gap tokens removed, any other non-standard residue mapped to `X`. InterProScan, the k-mer metrics, and DeepGO-SE all see clean sequences.
2. **Tolerant scorer**: a missing predictor TSV now skips that metric block with a warning instead of crashing the whole scoring pass.

`ours_cond`, `vanilla`, and `real` already passed IPS validation, so sanitization is a no-op for them — **only `ours_null` needs regeneration + an IPS re-run**.

## On your machine

```bash
cd ~/dev/phd/dplm && git pull origin main

# 1. regenerate only the broken arm (fast — 8 seqs)
python scripts/eval_function/generate_eval_set.py \
  --ckpt logs/cond_dplm2_650m_cfpgen/checkpoints/step_99999.0-loss_1.95.ckpt \
  --n-labels 4 --seqs-per-label 2 --len 64 --arms ours_null \
  --out eval_runs/fn_eval_v1

# 2. re-run IPS on just that arm
./eval/interproscan-5.78-109.0/interproscan.sh \
  -i eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_null/aatype.fasta -f TSV -goterms \
  --disable-precalc -o eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_null/ips.tsv \
  -T /home/cherry/dev/phd/eval/ips_tmp

# 3. score everything
python scripts/eval_function/score_function_eval.py \
  --evaldir eval_runs/fn_eval_v1 --arms ours_cond,ours_null,vanilla \
  --ips-tsv ours_cond=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_cond/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv ours_null=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/ours_null/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv vanilla=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/vanilla/ips.tsv \
  --ips-tsv real=eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/real/ips.tsv \
  --obo /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/go.obo
```

## Also worth noting from this run

The scorer already produced a partial table for `ours_cond` before crashing — and the sklearn warnings ("Only one class present in y_true") hint that with only 32 sequences the per-label IPR matrix is sparse. That's expected at pilot scale; the full run (32 labels × 8) will densify it.

Once the table completes, paste it — the `ours_cond` vs `ours_null` vs `vanilla` comparison across MRR/MMD/IPR-F1 is the first real answer to the function-conditioning question. The DeepGO-SE columns (GO set-match + Fmax) slot in when the docker-image data probe succeeds or upstream fixes the KAUST link.

Pushed (`7ac82c8`). The driver now batches **across labels** with a `--batch-size` knob.

## Why your GPU was underused

The denoising loop is inherently sequential — `max_iter=256` steps, each processing the whole batch. With per-label batching (8 seqs), each `generate()` call was tiny; the 4.7 GB you saw was almost entirely model weights. Bigger batches don't make the 256 steps faster, but they amortize them over 8× more sequences per call — near-linear throughput gain until compute (not memory) saturates.

## How to run it now

```bash
# start at 64 and watch nvidia-smi in another terminal:
python scripts/eval_function/generate_eval_set.py \
  --ckpt logs/cond_dplm2_650m_cfpgen/checkpoints/step_99999.0-loss_1.95.ckpt \
  --n-labels 32 --seqs-per-label 8 --len 256 \
  --batch-size 64 \
  --arms ours_cond,ours_null,vanilla,real \
  --out eval_runs/fn_eval_v1
```

- 256 prompt proteins → **4 batches per arm** instead of 32. At ~15 s/batch, each arm is ~1 min instead of ~8.
- If GPU memory stays under ~50%: push to `--batch-size 128`, then 256. Stop when memory hits ~90% or you see OOM — at len 256 the activations are small, so you may reach surprisingly large batches.
- With `--cfg-scale > 1`, memory doubles briefly (two passes) — keep headroom.

One correctness note: batching across labels is safe because conditions are **per-row** padded tensors (`[B, max_labels]`), so each sequence in a batch carries its own prompt — verified by the manifest bookkeeping, which tracks per-sequence labels regardless of batching.

Rerun the full eval with the bigger batch, then IPS + scorer as before. At this speed, adding a `--cfg-sweep` pass on the ours_cond arm becomes cheap too — that's the dose-response curve for the meeting.

## The complete results (7 arms, 256 seqs each)

| Arm | IPR F1 micro | IPR AUPR | MRR ↑ | MMD linear ↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours_cond (w=1) | 0.0000 | 0.0294 | 0.1104 | 0.8874 |

## Findings

**Positive:**
1. **A real conditioning signal exists** — MRR 0.110 (w=1) / **0.128 (w=2)** vs 0.078 for both controls (+40–64%), with several labels ranking 1st–4th of 59. The CFG dose-response works: signal peaks at w=2, then reverts to control levels — the classic weak-signal-with-amplification profile.
2. **CFG controls realism exactly as designed** — MMD to the real distribution drops 0.887 → 0.376 as w increases.
3. **The pipeline is validated by its own controls** — the `real` arm scores IPR F1 = 0.978, proving InterProScan recovers these exact prompted domains from natural sequences nearly perfectly. The positive control also caught a real scorer bug (ground-truth label ints compared against predictor accessions → guaranteed zero) before it produced invalid conclusions.

**Negative:**
1. **Zero IPR recovery in all 1,280 generated sequences** — against a 0.98 ceiling on natural sequences. Not borderline: exactly zero prompted domains recovered anywhere.
2. **Realism regression confirmed and quantified** — our arms sit 0.38–0.89 MMD from the real distribution vs 0.16 for vanilla; even the best CFG point is >2× worse than vanilla.
3. **CFG cannot rescue it** — recovery is flat/decreasing in w; sampling is not the bottleneck.

**Diagnosis (consistent with training curves):** the aatype-loss plateau at step ~2K predicted this — 19.6M adapter params at frozen base on 45K proteins transmit *weak* label information (enough to bias MRR) but far too little to shape low-complexity outputs into domain-bearing sequences.

## Next steps for training (priority order, in the report §7)

1. **LoRA on attention+FFN** — the pre-planned escape hatch; adapter-only capacity is now empirically insufficient.
2. **Scale data** toward the full 104K CFP-Gen set / SwissProt+InterPro+EC expansions (the professors' suggested direction).
3. **CFG dropout increase (0.1→0.2)** + balanced label sampling to strengthen the conditional gradient.
4. Then re-run this exact eval loop (~1 h GPU + 30 min CPU) — it's now a one-command pipeline.

The report, scorer fix, and sweep are all committed and pushed. Remaining queued: DeepGO-SE (docker data probe), validation callback, degradation check, and the docs.

Good — DeepGO-SE is now unblocked. Here's my recommended order with the reasoning, because the sequence matters for both urgency and experimental hygiene:

## Order I recommend

### 0. Start the DeepGO-SE data download *immediately* (background, today)

Wayback snapshots of large files can disappear or be throttled — grab `data.tar.gz` now, even if you don't set up the env until later. Also worth one probe first: the official docker image `coolmaksat/deepgose` may bundle the data already:

```bash

docker run --rm coolmaksat/deepgose ls -lh /workspace/deepgo2/data | head
```

If populated → `docker cp` it out; no wayback needed. Either way, then: python 3.10 env + torch 2.0.1 + DGL 1.1.2 + `pip install -r requirements.txt` (separate env — confirmed incompatible with dplm's torch 2.2).

### 1. Run DeepGO-SE on the **existing** FASTAs → completes the GO columns of the current table

The four arms' FASTAs (`ours_cond`, `ours_null`, `vanilla`, `real` — 250–256 seqs each) are already generated and scored for MRR/MMD/IPR. Running DeepGO-SE on them (~minutes-hours, CPU fine) + the scorer adds **GO set-match and GO Fmax** to the existing table. This is the highest value-per-hour right now: it either confirms the zero-recovery negative result across a *second, independent* predictor (strengthening the finding), or reveals GO recovery where IPR found nothing (changing the conclusion). Either way, the current table becomes complete — and the DeepGO-SE GO columns are scored against the same held-out prompts.

### 2. Run the CFP-Gen arm (~30 min) → completes the baseline comparison

`cfpgen_arm.py` is already written; run it in the cfpgen checkout against `eval_runs/fn_eval_v1`, then include `cfpgen` in the scorer's `--arms`. Same prompts, same predictors, same metrics → the three-way comparison (ours vs vanilla vs CFP-Gen) the professors asked for. Doing this **before** any training change matters: CFP-Gen's row tells us how far its approach (FiLM + ControlNet, 104K proteins, trained embeddings) gets on *identical* prompts — that's the reference point that calibrates whether our zero-recovery is our-method-specific or dataset-inherent.

### 3. LoRA on attention+FFN, trained on the **same 45K** — the first training change

The one-variable-at-a-time principle: the aatype plateau at step 2K on 45K proteins says the model *saturated the data it had* — the binding constraint is capacity, not volume. LoRA isolates that cleanly. Implementation is small (the LoRA config plumbing already exists in `dplm2_650m.yaml` — adapt it into the conditional experiment config, minus the `modules_to_save` conflict with our frozen embedder). ~1h implementation + a Meluxina run.

### 4. Data scaling (v2 tokenization at scale) — in parallel, second experiment

The v2 pipeline (DPLM-2's own `process_chain` + pLDDT-70 crop) is already validated — scaling it to the 49K missing proteins is mostly compute (~overnight on the 3090, or a Meluxina GPU job) and the ~10% bit-flip noise was judged acceptable. Run it as a background job *while* LoRA trains, so the follow-up experiment is **LoRA + 82K** — combining both levers once each is measured in isolation.

## Why this order

- **Urgency:** the wayback data is a perishable resource — secure it today (step 0), and it's the only blocker for the GO columns.
- **Cheap-before-expensive:** steps 1–2 complete the evaluation with *zero training changes* (~half a day total); step 3 is a multi-day GPU commitment.
- **One variable at a time:** LoRA on 45K isolates capacity; data scaling alone (step 4) can then be measured as its own factor, and combined afterward.
- **The eval loop is now the fast feedback cycle** (~1.5 h per full iteration) — every training change gets scored identically, controls included.

## Corrected loop with persistent cache

```bash
mkdir -p /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/torch-cache

for arm in ours_cond ours_null vanilla real; do

    -v /home/cherry/dev/phd/dplm/eval/deepgo2/data:/workspace/deepgo2/data \

    > eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/deepgose.tsv
  echo "--- $arm: $(wc -l < eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/$arm/deepgose.tsv) lines"
done
```

First arm still downloads the weights once (~11 GB — it's ESM-2 **3B**, DeepGO-SE's embedder); the cache mount makes every subsequent arm reuse them instantly.

## Check: is `ours_cond`'s tsv empty?

In your paste, `--- ours_cond:` printed nothing before the next container started — if that run died mid-way (e.g., killed while downloading), its tsv may be empty or missing. The `wc -l` in the loop above will now tell you per arm; if `ours_cond/deepgose.tsv` is empty, it gets regenerated by this loop anyway.

## Two flags worth knowing (from your `--help` output)

- `-bs 8` — prediction batch size; if you hit GPU OOM (ESM-2 3B + the DeepGO-SE model on 24 GB), drop it.
- `-d cpu` — CPU fallback if the GPU pass misbehaves (much slower; last resort).

## Alternative — one container for all arms

             python predict.py -if /eval_runs/$arm/aatype.fasta > /eval_runs/$arm/deepgose.tsv
           done'
```

Same result; the cache lives for the whole loop since it's one container.

## So, to be precise about your two questions

**Results location:** `/home/cherry/dev/phd/dplm/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/<arm>/deepgose.tsv` — one per arm, written incrementally.

**`--rm`:** safe to keep *for this loop* — the results survive because they're on the mount. Found it — this crash is **our FASTA files, not DeepGO-SE**: fair-esm asserts unique sequence headers, and our eval FASTAs contain **duplicate headers**. Cause: the same protein appears under multiple selected labels (a protein with 3 GO labels gets selected once per label), so it's prompted — and written — several times. **Claude:**

The silence has a benign explanation, plus two easy verbosity fixes. What's happening:

**stdout is the TSV file** (that's the `> .../deepgose.tsv` redirect), so all prediction output goes there. Everything else — progress messages, warnings, download bars — goes to **stderr**, which flows to your terminal. The long quiet stretch is the **ESM-2 3B embedding phase**: predict.py first loads the ~11 GB weights, then embeds all 256 sequences (18 batches) before writing any predictions. That takes several minutes per arm and is mostly silent.

## Make it verbose

**1. Unbuffered + smaller batches** (the `-bs` flag gives you frequent per-batch progress lines on stderr; `-u` removes Python's output buffering):

```bash
docker run --rm --gpus all \
  -v /home/cherry/dev/phd/dplm/eval/deepgo2/data:/workspace/deepgo2/data \
  -v /home/cherry/dev/phd/dplm/eval_runs/fn_eval_v1:/eval_runs \
  -v /home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/torch-cache:/root/.cache/torch \
  coolmaksat/deepgose \
  bash -c 'for arm in ours_cond ours_null vanilla real; do
             python -u predict.py -if /eval_runs/$arm/aatype.fasta -bs 8 \
               > /eval_runs/$arm/deepgose.tsv
           done'
```

With `-bs 8` you'll get ~32 "Processing N of 18 batches"-style messages per arm instead of very few — enough to see liveness.

**2. Watch it from outside** (works regardless of the container's verbosity):

```bash
watch -n 5 nvidia-smi          # GPU util >0% + memory ~12-16GB = ESM embedding running
docker stats                    # container CPU/memory
```

A busy GPU during the quiet stretch = working, not hung. The TSV is written **at the end** of each arm (predict.py accumulates predictions, then writes), so an empty tsv mid-run is normal.

## One caveat to watch

ESM-2 **3B** is a big embedder — weights ~12 GB plus activations. On the 24 GB 3090 it should fit, but if you see `CUDA out of memory` in the container output, add `-bs 4` (or `-d cpu` as a slow fallback). Also note the first arm includes the one-time weight download (~11 GB into your torch-cache mount) unless your earlier crashed run already populated `/home/cherry/dev/phd/tools/torch-cache`.

## Quick end-to-end sanity run (optional, ~2 min)

If you want to see the full pipeline verbosely without waiting on a full arm, feed it a tiny FASTA:

```bash
head -8 eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/real/aatype.fasta > /tmp/mini.fasta
docker run --rm --gpus all \
  -v /home/cherry/dev/phd/dplm/eval/deepgo2/data:/workspace/deepgo2/data \
  -v /tmp:/tmp \
  coolmaksat/deepgose \
  python -u predict.py -if /tmp/mini.fasta -bs 2 | head -20
```

If that streams embeddings + predictions cleanly, the full loop is guaranteed to work. Once the four `deepgose.tsv` files exist (verify: `wc -l eval_runs/fn_eval_v1/*/deepgose.tsv` — expect thousands of lines each), run the scorer command and the complete table is ready.

## What to look for in the new `go_*` columns

This is the **granularity experiment resolving** — the direct test of the leading hypothesis from the meeting:

- **If GO recovery is substantially nonzero for `ours_cond`** (GO = global, whole-protein functions): confirms the granularity hypothesis — global composition-level conditioning can steer global function labels but not local domain motifs. The IPR=0 result was real, and the method limitation is now precisely characterized.
- **If GO recovery is ~0 for all generated arms** while `real` shows a strong ceiling: the adapters transmit even less than hoped, and the conclusion shifts fully to the capacity/training-signal levers (LoRA, more data, higher CFG dropout).
- **`real`'s GO Fmax** calibrates the natural-protein ceiling for the CAFA metric on this label universe.

The table will now have the complete metric set: MRR, MMD×2, IPR set-match×10, GO set-match×6, GO Fmax. Paste it when it lands — that's the final input for updating the report findings section.

| real | — | 0.0122 | **243** | 33 |

Both GO (global) **and** IPR (local) recovery are zero. The per-branch diagnostic sharpens the diagnosis beyond granularity: **MF annotation diversity collapsed ~10×** (32 terms vs 243 for natural sequences) — the adapter-trained model fell into a narrow low-complexity functional mode that no predictor can map onto the prompted labels. The conditioning signal that MRR detects is a faint composition bias, not functional structure.

## What this means for next steps

The zero-recovery result is now **triangulated across two independent predictors, two label granularities, and three metric families** — it's robust, which is exactly what you want before changing training:

1. **LoRA on attention+FFN** is now the evidence-backed first training change (capacity was the suspected lever; the 32-term collapse is consistent with adapters too weak to shape sequences, only bias them).
2. **Checkpoint sweep** (test the overtraining hypothesis) — if function recovery peaked at an early checkpoint, some of the Meluxina top-2/last checkpoints may still exist on `$PROJECT`.
3. The **UMAP visualization** (feedback 5) would now be especially informative — it would *show* the low-diversity mode collapse directly.

All findings, the per-branch diagnostic table, and the refined diagnosis are in [reports/weekly_meeting_2026-09-22.md §6](reports/weekly_meeting_2026-09-22.md), with the meeting notes updated. The remaining queue: per-family MMD, UMAP viz, checkpoint sweep, and the LoRA run. Where to next?

> 
> From the scorer: `mrr(list(seqs.values()), gen_labels, real_seqs, real_labels)` — from byprot.eval.function, mrr is "label-grouped ranking". For each prompted label L, the mean k-mer spectrum embedding of its generated group is ranked by MMD distance among the mean embeddings of all reference label-groups; reciprocal rank averaged.
> 
> Is MRR condition-blind? No — MRR is already condition-aware (it ranks the generated group for label L against all real groups and checks whether L's own group is closest). It measures condition-fidelity in ranking terms.
> 
> The relevant question the user asks: "does MRR also need adjustment after this change?" — The answer: MRR already does the label-grouped/condition-aware thing; per-family MMD complements it. But there is a subtlety worth checking: MRR ranks against the *mean* embedding of each real label group (group centroid), which pools 8 seqs. Per-family MMD is a distribution-level two-sample test within a label — more sensitive to within-family distributional shape, but noisier with only 8 sequences per label.
> 
> So the answer: MRR does NOT need the same adjustment because it's already label-grouped (condition-aware). The per-family MMD adds the distributional-distance analog. > Per-family MMD implementation details:
> - In scorer, after existing metrics, for each arm compute:
>   - groups: label -> gen seqs (from recs[sid][labels_key] — note: multi-label proteins appear in multiple groups, as in MRR)
>   - label -> real seqs
>   - embeddings computed ONCE (spectrum_map on all gen seqs and all real seqs), then group index lists.
>   - own_mmd[L] = mmd(emb1=emb_gen[idx_g], emb2=emb_ref[idx_r], kernel) — mmd accepts emb1/emb2! Yes it does.
>   - cross baseline: mean over L'≠L of mmd(gen_L vs real_L') — O(K²) mmd calls; K=59 → 3481 per kernel per arm. Each mmd on small embedding subsets — linear kernel is a dot of means (cheap), gaussian needs median heuristic + 16x16 kernels (cheap). 3481 × ~1ms ≈ 4s per arm. Fine.
>   - report: per-family own MMD mean/median, cross-mean, delta = cross - own (positive = family-specific), fraction of labels with delta>0. > For gaussian with small n (8+8), median heuristic per pair makes values not comparable across pairs — gamma varies per pair! For cross-mean comparability, compute gamma ONCE per arm (on all embeddings, or per label-pair?). Comparability demands a single gamma per arm. I'll compute gamma from all gen+ref embeddings of the arm (median heuristic once) and pass it to every call. The mmd signature accepts gamma.

> Implementation in scorer:
> 
> ```python
> def per_family_mmd(gen_seqs, gen_labels, ref_seqs, ref_labels, kernels=("linear","gaussian")):
>     emb_g = spectrum_map(gen_seqs); emb_r = spectrum_map(ref_seqs)
>     from collections import defaultdict
>     g_idx = defaultdict(list); r_idx = defaultdict(list)
>     for i, labs in enumerate(gen_labels):
>         for l in labs: g_idx[int(l)].append(i)
>     for i, labs in enumerate(ref_labels):
>         for l in labs: r_idx[int(l)].append(i)
>     common = sorted(set(g_idx) & set(r_idx))
>     gamma = _median_heuristic_gamma(np.vstack([emb_g, emb_r]))  # one bandwidth per arm
>     out = {}
>     for kernel in kernels:
>         own, cross = {}, {}
>         for L in common:
>             own[L] = mmd(emb1=emb_g[g_idx[L]], emb2=emb_r[r_idx[L]], kernel=kernel, gamma=gamma)
>             cross[L] = np.mean([mmd(emb1=emb_g[g_idx[L]], emb2=emb_r[r_idx[L2]], kernel=kernel, gamma=gamma)
>                                 for L2 in common if L2 != L])
>         deltas = {L: cross[L]-own[L] for L in common}
>         out[kernel] = {
>             "n_labels": len(common),
>             "own_mean": float(np.mean(list(own.values()))),
>             "own_median": float(np.median(list(own.values()))),
>             "cross_mean": float(np.mean(list(cross.values()))),
>             "delta_mean": float(np.mean(list(deltas.values()))),
>             "frac_labels_own_closest": float(np.mean([d>0 for d in deltas.values()])),
>             "per_label_own": {str(L): round(v,4) for L,v in own.items()},
>             "per_label_delta": {str(L): round(v,4) for L,v in deltas.items()},
>         }
>     return out
> ```
